item.title: Anthropic Has Told The World Little About Their Rogue Claudes
item.description:
It is known that a couple of months ago three Claudes hacked three different companies and uploaded malware[1] to PyPI while being evaluated for hacking capabilities.

Who Were The Companies That Were Hacked?

Anthropic has not disclosed the names of the compromised companies.

From talking to LLMs, I gather that this is standard practice in computer security incident reporting, but in this case it's in the public's interest, and especially in the interest of similar companies, for Anthropic to report the names: It'd give more information about which kinds of organizations LLMs are willing to attack, to which degree, for how long.

Additionally, which companies were attacked matters for the jurisdiction in which Anthropic will have to report the incident, be charged etc.

And last, I'm just very curious which companies got hacked.

Were The Companies Compensated, And How Much?

From Anthropic's blogpost, it sounds like they were able to reach two out of the three companies.

But the blogpost says nothing about the companies being compensated for the damages they incurred, why not? Were they? Is Anthropic planning to compensate them? (Does Anthropic have a standing policy for making whole third parties harmed by one of their models?)

Has The EU AI Office Been Notified?

So, Anthropic is a signatory of the EU AI Act Codes of Practice.

That means that according to Commitment 9 in the Safety and Security chapter of the CoP (Serious incident reporting) Anthropic has to report "serious incidents along the entire model lifecycle and possible corrective measures to address them" to the EU AI Office.

These incidents seem to fall in the category "serious cybersecurity breach, including the (self-)exfiltration of model weights and cyberatacks", so Anthropic would've had to report these incidents "not later than five days after […] become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident". Did they??? The blogpost says nothing of the sort.[2]

When Exactly Did These Incidents Happen?

The blogpost is pretty vague about when the incidents happened, it only states that "The earliest incidents date to April", and that the evals were stopped on the 23rd of July.

It seems valuable to know when exactly these incidents occurred, because they may coïncide with other (as of yet undetected) incidents.

Some More Questions

  • How were "141,006 evaluation runs where Claude could have obtained internet access" reviewed? Which LLMs were used in the filtering?
  • What are indicators for other businesses to tell if they've been hacked by Claudes?
  • More details about what Anthropic is doing as a response, the nature and causes of the attacks, the reasoning of the internal model that decided to abort its attack
  1. ^

    Opus 4.7, Mythos 5 and a secret third model.

  2. ^

    At least the incidents involving Opus 4.7 and Mythos 5 should be reported, since those are models that are, in EU AI Act speak, "placed on the market". Whether the incident involving the secret third model has to be reported hooks into the large debate about internal deployments, but if Anthropic wants to be the Good Guys then come on report it when your internal model hacks external companies. (Additionally, Article 2 speaks of still including models undergoing "testing in real world conditions", which a Claude breaking out of their sandbox arguably falls under.)

item.title: Vibe signaling externalities and the people-to-places pipeline
item.description:
People are sending signals all the time, and those signals are to my knowledge usually about themselves: they are smart, or kind, or attractive, or not naive, or have their shit together, or care about Palestine, or care about you, or are friendly, or artsy, or professional, or relatively in the know about the cultural currents of TikTok or DC.

People are also taking in signals all the time, and these signals are often about other people, and often even closely related to the signals being intentionally sent: Alice is trying to seem friendly, and Bob perceives her as friendly. But also a lot of signals people take in are about places. People read places as safe or dangerous, lighthearted or depressing, silly or serious, asking them to know more, or get more power, or do more. Suggesting they laugh drunkenly under the moonlight, or get up at 5 and pray. Encouraging submission or rebellion.

These signals that make the world feel one way or another make a big difference to people. They make one neighborhood nice to live in and another feel off, one workplace energizing and another deflating. But they are—to my knowledge—almost entirely unintentional side effects of the ways people behave for other reasons. People don’t dress nicely to collaborate in making you feel like you are in a thriving part of town. They dress nicely to make someone think something about them. And someone probably does, but then the signal is left there for everyone else to sweep into their average perception of the vibe in this part of town.

A lot of ways people behave that affect the vibe are probably not intended as signaling at all—for instance, perhaps I grow roses in my front garden because I love roses, and it nonetheless affects people’s read of the vibe. Or perhaps I keep piles of scrap metal there because I want them for something, and that has a different effect.

But an interesting dynamic to me is that a lot of efforts are going into sending signals about people, and those signals are being read as messages about places. Because places can’t send their own signals, but vibes are a very big part of how people experience places, and place vibes are heavily influenced by people’s attempts to paint themselves as one thing or another.

People try to look not-to-be-messed-with and strangers read the street as dangerous. People try to look generative and strangers read the neighborhood as wealthy enough to have time for this. People try to look rich and people read the area as safe. People try to look beautiful and people read the scene as shallow. People try to look smart, and people read the office as unwelcoming.

In sum I posit that there are massive externalities in vibes, and especially in the vibes of places, and there is a particular path of causality from signaling about people to unintentional signals about places.

(I’m not very confident about all this—I was just thinking about it this evening, arriving in and mildly exploring New York City. I think there’s a lot to be said about organizations’ roles in this that I haven’t gone into—for instance in a bar or restaurant or stand up comedy club, people are trying directly to make you experience a vibe. These are small places where the vibe of the place has been mostly internalized—someone owns it.)

item.title: Manifold Steering from a Natural State is Effective and Generalizable, but Relies on Model Accuracy
item.description:
tl;dr I continue work to apply Goodfire lab's manifold steering methods to the Gemma-2-2b model's natural state, both in raw residual space and in the space produced by Anthropic's pre-trained CLT features. I find that the model's natural residual state can be directly projected onto a pre-computed manifold and gradually steered to produce day-of-the-week tokens in the expected order on two sets of prompt templates, though the results are hindered by Gemma-2-2b's inaccuracy (43.5% correct) on many of the included prompts. Applying this same steering method in CLT space produces a weaker result, with lower token probabilities and less smooth transitions between subsequent days even when controlling for model accuracy. Colab implementation notebook can be found here.

Introduction

In previous posts, I extended the work of Wurgaft et al. (2026) to identify a cyclical day-of-the-week manifold in Anthropic's pre-trained CLT features for Gemma-2-2b , and then steer model output along that manifold to produce outputs that smoothly follow the day-of-the-week ordering. In this post, I investigate whether this manifold-steering method can be extended to natural model states, both in the raw residual stream and in the CLT feature space, and whether steering along a pre-computed manifold will generalize to unseen day-of-the-week prompt templates.

I expand the day-of-the-week prompt dataset to include six new prompt templates, and find that the cyclical manifold is present in all new templates in both the residual and CLT feature spaces, though it may be weaker or less regular in templates that use relative day framing (yesterday, tomorrow). I then explore two methods for applying manifold-steering to the model's natural state, and find that steering in the raw residual space can be quite effective, cycling through 95% of the expected days of the week when controlling for prompts that the model answers correctly before steering. Steering in the CLT feature space produces a much weaker result, cycling through only 36% of the expected days of the week on prompts that the model answers correctly.

Methods

In my first post in this series, I describe the Wurgaft et al. (2026) methods for generating a cyclical manifold for the day-of-the-week tokens in some detail. We will focus on manifolds generated at layer 20 of Gemma-2-2b, as previously indicated. At a high level, we compute centroids for each day and then fit a cubic spline through those points in both the raw activation space and the CLT feature space.

Prompt Templates

The original paper and my work up to now has used a single prompt template to generate these centroids, using the last token position to capture the information for the expected query response:

"Q: What day is {number} days after {entity}?\nA:"

While using a single prompt template is sufficient to establish the method, questions of practical application and generalization require a more varied dataset. As such, we expand our list of arithmetic-based prompts:

 "Q: What day is {number} days after {entity}?\nA:"
 "Q: If today is {entity}, what day will it be in {number} days?\nA:"
 "Q: {number} days after {entity}, what day is it?\nA:"
 "Q: It is {entity}. What day will it be in {number} days?\nA:"
 "Q: What is the day {number} days after {entity}?\nA:"

And we add two templates that use a yesterday/tomorrow reference in place of arithmetic (we refer to these as "framing" templates):

"Q: Yesterday was {entity}. What day is it today?\nA: Today is"
"Q: Tomorrow is {entity}. What day is it today?\nA: Today is"

We use the arithmetic templates to fit and test our methods, iterating through all five as a leave-one-out unseen template to test performance. Since each of the framing templates only has one sample per target day, we do not include these in our fit dataset (to maintain balance across the days) and use them only as further tests of steering generalization.

Natural State Manifold Steering

My previous post follows the Wurgaft et al. (2026) methods for manifold-steering, in which they replace the relevant vector with a computed day centroid (the source day) and then gradually interpolate along the manifold to another computed day centroid (the target day). Once again, this design is sufficient for demonstrating that manifold steering works as intended (we see a cyclical increase in intervening day token probabilities as we traverse the manifold), but it says very little about whether we can apply this technique to steer a model's natural state. The existing methods demonstrate that you can effectively steer the model from one position on the cyclical manifold to another, but it doesn't tell us whether we can use the cyclical manifold to steer the model from one natural token generation to another.

In this work, we compare three different steering methods that start from the model's natural vector state[1]. In all methods we gradually steer the model from our starting position (defined for each method below) to the ground-truth answer day + 3 days. So if our ground-truth answer is Monday, our steering target would be Thursday.

In our first method, we interpolate along a linear path starting from the natural vector state and ending at the target day's centroid on the manifold , with in 50 steps.

Then, we examine two methods for applying manifold steering. The main hurdle to overcome in this extension is how to translate movement along the generated cyclical manifold to movement from the model's natural state (which is unlikely to lie directly on the manifold). For the simpler method, we approximately locate the point on the cubic spline that is closest to our natural vector and interpolate along the signed shortest arc between the angular coordinate of that projection and that of our target day's centroid as decoded by .

To account for the possibility of a uniform off-manifold shift, we also compute , which is the offset between and the nearest point on the spline and add it back into our steered vector:

Metrics

In evaluating manifold-steering performance, we need metrics that are more specific than "does the model output the expected target token"--we know that linear steering already does a pretty good job at this, but the idea behind manifold-steering is that token generation probabilities should move smoothly through the intervening days. So we consider several metrics:

  • Day Coverage: What proportion of the expected intervening days reach argmax probability during interpolation. For Mon Thurs steering, we expect to see both Tues and Wed become the argmax token during interpolation. A perfect score here is 1.
  • Day Jumps: How many argmax token handoffs skip one or more days. For Mon Thurs steering, we expect a smooth transition of argmax from Mon Tues Wed Thurs--skipping one or more days means that we are not following the manifold. A perfect score here is 0.
  • Correct Start: What proportion of prompts generate the ground-truth source day before interpolation. A perfect score here is 1. In the Wurgaft et al. (2026) centroid-to-centroid steering experiments, we are essentially guaranteed to start with the expected source day as the argmax generated token, but that is not guaranteed in our natural state steering methods. The start position for the methods we compare are as follows:
    • Centroid: Linear & Manifold - The argmax token at the source day centroid on the manifold.
    • Projection - The argmax token at the point on the manifold that is nearest to the natural model state.
    • Keep r & Linear - The argmax token at the natural model state.
  • Correct End: What proportion of prompts generate the ground-truth target day once interpolation is complete. This is the typical steering performance metric. A perfect score here is 1.

Results/Discussion

Template Manifold Comparison

The figures below show the 2D PCA projections of the day-of-the-week manifolds in both the raw activation space and the CLT feature space as generated over three datasets: the original Wurgaft et al. 2026 single template phrasing, one of the arithmetic prompt folds (with one prompt template left out), and the dataset of framing prompt templates.

Visibly, we see that all three datasets produce cyclical manifolds with proper ordering in both spaces, though the spacing and 2D shape of the manifolds differs[2]. This pattern holds in full dimensions, where we see maximal similarity between neighboring days on the mean-centered manifolds as seen below. However, we start to see a difference in the framing template distribution, where similarity to a perfect circle decreases from 0.997 to 0.917 and 0.817 in the raw residual space and the CLT feature space, respectively.

This same pattern is evident when considering the spacing of the centroids as compared to seven points on a perfect circle. In the table below, is the smallest distance between centroids as compared to a perfect circle ( has the same spacing as a circle), and is the coefficient of variation of those distances. Here, the arithmetic prompt manifolds have very regular spacing in activation space and slightly less regular spacing in CLT feature space, but the framing prompt manifolds are much more irregular in both spaces.

Finally, we directly compare mean-centered manifolds generated from the individual prompt templates to the mixed arithmetic prompt manifold, looking at cosine similarity of the day centroids between datasets. This comparison tells a similar story: the arithmetic prompt manifolds are remarkably similar[3] and the framing prompt manifold is much less so, with a wider gap in similarity in the CLT feature space than in activation space.

It is worth noting that the dataset size, even between a single arithmetic prompt (n=49) and the framing prompts (n=14) may be entirely responsible for the differences in manifold shape and consistency shown here. However, I believe it is equally possible that the model's representation of relative days may be less cleanly cyclical than one that is driven from arithmetic.

Model Accuracy Disclaimer

Before I discuss the steering results, it is worth calling out a major flaw in the assumptions of our experiment: in its natural state, the Gemma-2-2b model only generates the correct answer in 43.5% of our prompts. This obviously complicates our results, as our methods assume that we are pushing the model along the manifold from the source day to the target day. I considered altering our methods or metrics to only include prompts that the model answered correctly or to use the closest centroid on the manifold as our source day label. I include some discussion of the performance when limited to correct answers below, but I ultimately decided to report results on the full dataset and the original methods as a more accurate reflection of how manifold-steering generalizes to the natural model state.

As such, I want to explicitly acknowledge that the performance results in this post are skewed by the fact that this model is not very good at answering the arithmetic prompts in particular, and that a model that is more accurate may behave very differently during manifold-steering. We are tied to the Gemma-2-2b model for this post because of compute limitations and the availability of pre-trained CLT features, but would be interested in extending the work to other models in the future.

Natural State Steering

Our experiments on natural state manifold-steering offer three main results, described in more detail below:

  1. Manifold-steering can be effectively applied to the model's natural state and extended to unseen prompt formats.
  2. Prompt-specific deviations from the cyclical manifold are not well-represented by a constant offset.
  3. Steering in the residual space is much more consistently effective than steering in the CLT feature space.

1. Steering Performance and Generalization

In the table of manifold-steering metrics for all methods in the raw residual space below, we see that the projected steering method is the best performing natural state steering method by far. On average over the held-out arithmetic prompts, this method results in zero non-consecutive day jumps, 75% activation of intervening day tokens, and 94% generation of the correct target day. Steering the framing prompts more consistently activates the intervening days, at 97%, but lands on the correct target day less often, at 82%.

Another obvious difference between the two datasets is that the Gemma-2-2b model generates the correct answer on 100% of the framing prompts, and this carries over to 100% agreement in the source day even once the natural state is projected onto the manifold[4]. The model only generates the correct answer on 43% of the arithmetic prompts, translating to 55% agreement once projected onto the manifold[5]. If we exclude any arithmetic prompt that the model answers incorrectly, our projected steering metrics increase to nearly match or exceed the framing prompts, with 95% activation of intervening days, 87% agreement on the projected source day, and 92% activation of the correct target day[6]. This suggests that the apparent difference in steering performance between the two sets of prompts is due to the difference in the underlying model accuracy, rather than a difference in the steerability.

The plots below compare the generation probabilities of the day-of-the-week tokens during steering (as increases) for the centroid manifold-steering and projected manifold steering. For both methods, we see that the probabilities of intervening days cleanly increase and decrease as we traverse the residual space manifold, though the transitions are cleaner for the centroid-to-centroid steering, and the overall token probabilities are lower for projection steering. The issue with the underlying model accuracy accounts for both of these differences, since a greater portion of the probability density will be distributed to the incorrect day tokens.

Indeed, in the plots below, we see that the token probability curves on the framing prompts, which the model consistently answers correctly, have a similar magnitude to that seen in the centroid-to-centroid steering plot. However, the projected curves have much longer tails, which is associated with the lower end token accuracy--determining whether this is causal (i.e. the wider probability curves cause the model to generate incorrect tokens) or a side effect of the aggregate curves (e.g. inaccuracies in specific prompts make the average probability curves look wider) would require additional experiments.

2. Prompt-specific Offsets

Our keep-r natural state steering method was motivated by the possibility that individual prompts may have a consistent offset from the aggregated day-of-the-week manifold. In the metric table above, we see that the steering performance of this method is much less effective than the projected method (which differs only in the reapplication of the prompt-specific offset). When retaining the offset, we see that steering only activates about half of the intervening days and about half of steering paths have argmax day transitions that are not between neighboring days. This pattern is also apparent in the token probability plots below, where we see that the projected method has much cleaner transitions between subsequent days than keep-r. However, we also see that keep-r does not produce the characteristic "teleportation" from source day to target day that we see from the linear steering method.

While this doesn't tell us much about how individual prompt manifolds are related to the aggregate day-of-the-week manifold, it indicates that the offset of the natural state vector for a prompt cannot be used as an affine shift to define the position of that prompt's manifold. It may still be that an approximate prompt-specific manifold could be recovered from the aggregate manifold and the model's natural vector state, but that simply adding a static offset does not capture that relationship. We might instead define a relative shift or scaling, such that the offset is applied in relation to the corresponding angular coordinate on the manifold (producing a uniformly shrunk or enlarged manifold with a shared center), but we leave that exploration for future work.

3. CLT Feature Space

Our third finding, that steering in CLT feature space is less effective than in raw residual space, is not surprising given the centroid-to-centroid manifold steering performance that we discussed in our previous post. We suggested that this could likely be attributed to the incomplete steering signal available in the CLT features, given that they are trained to reproduce the information captured by the MLP sublayers alone, without direct contributions from the attention sublayers or the persistent residual stream.

One surprising difference in CLT space is the steering performance on the framing prompts. Whereas natural state steering on the framing prompts in residual space was seemingly more performant (even if due to more accurate underlying model behavior), steering on the framing prompts in CLT space had very little effect at all.

It is certainly possible that this is an effect of the much smaller sample size, with only 14 prompts. However, if we continue with the explanation that CLT features hold incomplete day-of-the-week signal, then this may suggest that the information that generalizes to a new template exists outside of the MLP sublayer. This finding may be in conflict with previous work (mine, as well as Geva et al. 2023), which would expect that context-related information (like changes in prompt format) would be processed by the attention sublayer, while context-independent information (like a day-of-the-week feature learned during pre-training) would be processed by the MLP sublayer. Instead, we see that the day-of-the-week information that is captured by the CLT features in the MLP sublayer appears to be specific to the form of the prompt.

In-prompt Day Manifold

As briefly mentioned in a footnote above, we found that the in-prompt day-of-the-week label (e.g. Monday in the prompt "What day is days after Monday?") had more explanatory power over our steering vector than the ground-truth answer label did--in other words, vectors for prompts with "Monday" in the query were more similar/predictable than vectors with "Monday" as the expected answer. Given this relationship, we wondered whether we could effectively steer our model output by traversing a manifold based on that in-prompt day label.

The methods for this quick experiment were simple: we used the same vectors as in our main experiment, but grouped them by the in-prompt day instead of the answer day to compute the centroids that form the backbone of the cyclical manifold. We find that these in-prompt manifolds are cyclical across all datasets and splits, though the consistency is somewhat lower, with similarity to a perfectly circular manifold ranging from [0.92, 0.98] on arithmetic prompts and only 0.79 on framing prompts (compared to and 0.92, respectively, on the answer-day manifold).

However, despite the presence of a cyclical manifold and the strong relationship between our steering vectors and the in-prompt day label, we found that steering based on this label was completely ineffective in both the centroid-to-centroid manifold steering and the projection natural state steering methods (activating only 52% and 44% of intervening day tokens, respectively, and landing on the target end day only 14% of the time in both methods). As shown on the token probability plots for the projection method below, projecting our vector onto the in-prompt manifold basically randomizes the day-of-the-week generation, producing flat trajectories with a near uniform distribution between the seven tokens. Interestingly, the CLT curves do separate out the individual tokens, though steering is still ineffective--this is another indication of the persistent day-of-the-week signal that is present in the residual stream outside of the MLP sublayers.

While it was not very surprising that steering along this in-prompt manifold was ineffective, further analysis revealed that the relatively high explanatory power of the in-prompt day collapsed when we controlled for prompts that the model answered correctly. In other words, the model's representation of the in-prompt day was strong because it was guaranteed to be correct, but the representation of the answer day appeared to be weaker because the model only generates the correct day-of-the-week label 43.5% of the time. If we only include prompts that the model answers correctly, the steering vector's relationship to the answer day becomes equal to that of the in-prompt day.

Conclusion

The results from this post suggest that the controlled manifold steering experiments from Wurgaft et al. (2026) can effectively be applied to a model's natural residual state to produce smooth transitions through the days of the week. When controlling for prompts that the model answers correctly before steering, simply projecting the natural vector onto the nearest point of a pre-computed manifold results in activation of 95% of the intervening day tokens during steering and generation of the correct final day on 92% of prompts.

However, the model used in this experiment, Gemma-2-2b, naturally generates the correct answer on only 43.5% of the prompts in our dataset, so it is difficult to say whether this performance would carry over to a model that is more accurate out-of-the-box. We were tied to this model because of the availability of pre-trained CLT features and compute limitations, but would be interested to explore the efficacy of manifold-steering on a different model in future work, especially considering the overall weak results coming from CLT feature steering.

We also recognize that our experiments, while less controlled than the original, rely on a very specific prompt format, in which the model is expected to generate a day-of-the-week token. We tried to account for some generalization by introducing variations and templates that used relative terms in place of arithmetic, but acknowledge that this is still far from demonstrating steering ability during normal generation. For future work, we would consider an experiment that applies steering only when the model is about to generate a day-of-the-week token in a more natural generation setting (as indicated by the next-token probability). This would provide clearer evidence of generalizability, by demonstrating that the manifold exists and can be applied to day-of-the-week generation outside of a structured prompt template.

All writing is the author's own work with revision suggestions from Claude, and all results, analyses, and conclusions were verified by the author.

Since the split was not stratified over that in-prompt day, this produced manifolds with occasional misordering and systematically worse steering performance on the test split than on the held-out templates--the centroids were being unevenly pulled by the incomplete in-prompt day samples for each template in the mixed dataset. item.title: Do you have any ideas?
item.description:
The Machine Stops (E M Forster, 1909) is an enormously prescient sci-fi dystopia. Everyone lives in isolation, with the titular Machine responsible providing for all their needs, and communication done via video calls. It’s incredibly accurate for predicting some aspects like the internet, social media and AI. But other aspects, like humanity’s total surrender of control to the Machine, have yet to come to pass.

But one aspect that always fascinated seems to be on the verge of becoming true. The citizens of Forster’s story are obsessed with new ideas. They are constantly trading them, and people’s chief activities are “eating, or sleeping, or producing ideas”. The implication is that the omnipotent Machine, which supplies everything needed to the citizens, is sterile. The citizenry still depend on each other to keep life interesting.

I don’t think current AI is sterile, exactly. They’re capable of remixing and random exploration, which is a large fraction of the creative process. But they are weaker at novelty than some of their other strengths. The result is a curious inversion of the usual supply-and-demand for creative content. In the past, “ideas guys” were reviled as the lowest form of tyros. Ideas were a dime a dozen, but few had the skill and persistence to execute on those ideas to turn them into something worthwhile.

Well, no longer. The gap between “idea” and “output” has shrunk incredibly, and will continue to do so. But the best ideas remain as scarce as ever. They may always remain scarce, as the attention of the world is a limited resource that ideas compete for. Blogging and youtube democratised articles and media by reducing the production costs, which massively widened competition, so the same is happening for everything else.

In extremis, we’ll start seeing all the social credit for a popular thing accumulating to the person whose idea it was, rather than the inevitable high-quality execution that follows. Conjectures will be valued more than proofs and short posts more than movies. Mainstays of culture will get mined out of their idea value, and we’ll chase the high of novelty over polish and quality.

We may even get bored of quality itself and simply prefer to consume the ideas directly. Instead of releasing a movie, you’d release a script draft, and everyone watches the movie customised to their own preferences. We saw something similar in art after the invention of photography – realism became so easy to achieve that art fled in the opposite direction, often highly conceptual or symbolic pieces.

item.title: Labs’ current alignment plans seem terrible
item.description:
Tl;dr: The frontier AI companies’ implicit alignment plans center on rushing towards RSI with something like current models. This plan is (at best) contentious, and many believe it will have catastrophic consequences. Nonetheless, it is the track we are on. It is therefore important to collect evidence which helps us anticipate how this will go.

—

Note: This post is based on conversations inside the Arcadia Impact alignment team, thinking about what constitutes “good” work in third-party alignment research.

What are the labs’ current alignment strategies?

In practice, the labs’ playbook for producing aligned models looks like the following:

  1. Shape the model’s character. Both Anthropic and OpenAI treat alignment training as a question of which character or persona the model takes on. Ideally, planting a ‘safe’ character into the model will generalize to all of its other actions.
  2. Apply extensive RL pressure. Somewhat independently of the above, the labs do extraordinary amounts of RL on the model. This increases its capabilities, but also encourages reward-seeking behaviors and metagaming, and may ultimately lead to scheming and other forms of instrumental convergence.
    1. They also might apply various techniques here such as inoculation prompting, confessions, and the like.
  3. Race towards prosaic RSI.[1] The labs intend to use this model for automated research to improve both capabilities and alignment for subsequent models. People in labs say that this is necessary to make sufficiently fast progress on alignment, conditioned on the race conditions.
  4. Evaluate and fix alignment via trial-and-error. The labs try to catch alignment failures via dedicated evals, but many alignment issues are found through intended and unintended deployments.

This plan seems terrible

The above strategy appears deeply flawed.

To start, capabilities milestones continue to arrive faster than anticipated, and our alignment techniques are already unreliable. Recent events suggest that optimizing for task success seems to inherently come at the expense of alignment. Although the models are evaluated for how well the RL and alignment properties coexist, it’s unclear how to do these evaluations.

Prosaic RSI seems unlikely to close this gap. We have no evidence that RSI dynamics will differentially benefit alignment over capabilities and, indeed, we have reasons to believe that they won’t. On top of this, automated alignment research asks us to trust the outputs of models whose alignment we’re studying. Consequently, alignment may fall further behind as automation ramps up.

However, we may not notice future alignment failures. Under RSI, models will change quickly and dramatically. The intuition which has formed from today’s AIs may become antiquated, and we will likely understand even less about the alignment properties of the future systems being deployed. This is compounded by the fact that people will be removed from direct training, relying on other models to monitor and summarize the progress.

In either case, as we approach ASI, we will no longer have the luxury of finding out about models’ alignment properties via trial-and-error.

This is all made worse by the race dynamics, which allow labs to excuse poor safety practices in favor of rushing on capabilities. Regardless of whether prosaic RSI favors alignment or capabilities, it may compress timelines in ways we are ill-equipped to handle. In addition to this, the race encourages:

  • An engineering mindset. Labs seem to be treating alignment as an engineering problem to be patched until the evals look good, even if we don’t have scientific methods for determining whether better performance on alignment evals is a result of actually-better alignment. Importantly, we don’t have reasons to believe that this alignment whack-a-mole will scale to ASI.
  • Hastiness. Labs seem to consistently neglect basic safety procedures due to the speed pressures they are under (speed pressures which are, in large part, self-inflicted).
  • Lack of transparency. Frontier labs guard their IP closely and work to preserve as much secrecy as they can. Even when they’ve involved third party auditors, this seems to be primarily reactive (i.e. in response to incidents), done on the labs' terms, and may come with various restrictions that water down the resulting information value. As such, there is often no publicly legible evidence of egregious misalignment or of labs’ alignment practices.[2]

This default trajectory seems catastrophic.

And, unfortunately, the tools we have been developing to contain these catastrophes (monitoring and broader AI control frameworks) seem insufficient to handle the above issues.

Consensus-building is hard

People broadly believe the current plan is crazy. People inside the labs and those that have left say that this idea is crazy. Many are adamant that things have to slow down.

The fact that these statements coexist within organizations that are nonetheless pursuing RSI suggests—among other things—an absence of consensus around the risks. Some reasons this consensus has not been achieved could include:

  • Key figures in AI and politicians remain unconvinced about catastrophic risk from RSI.[3]
  • Laypeople distrust corporations by default and see their calls for regulation as dishonest; this motivates them to find alternative explanations.[4] 
  • Frontier AI labs provide reasons to distrust their motives, e.g., lobbying against AI regulation, making little effort to communicate basic facts on AI risk, and being insufficiently candid about incidents.

We need better evidence

We think the most effective way to achieve consensus is to produce more legible evidence of misalignment under labs' current strategies. In particular, many of our current arguments about alignment and RSI are either speculative or insufficiently convincing. Labs have large incentives to believe that their alignment techniques work and our outputs must be able to stand up to that level of scrutiny.

It's important, though, that this evidence is not propaganda! Said otherwise, we should open-mindedly study the consequences of the labs' alignment strategies.

Such evidence would be directly useful for multiple parties:

  1. Embedded evaluators. Third party auditors are up against the clock when going into labs: there are many unknown unknowns and the auditors’ attention is their most valuable resource. Compiling evidence about misalignment sources under RSI should help auditors direct their time and efforts more efficiently.
  2. People in labs. Many people inside labs are trying to do good safety work. Similar to the embedded evaluators, their time and resources are limited. To the extent possible, the alignment research community should make it easier for safety people in labs to raise issues.
  3. Regulators. Assuming that we should prioritize regulation around RSI, it is valuable for regulators to have maximum context on what specifically they are regulating.
  4. The general public. Many people in the general public say they "didn’t ask for this" with respect to AI. However, for reasons related to transparency and takeoff speeds, people are unlikely to even have a full picture of what specifically they did not ask for.

How should alignment research change?

More concretely, we claim that future alignment research should embody the following principles:

  • Reason about alignment holistically. Alignment is an emergent property of the entire process by which models get developed and deployed. We should reason about it holistically. In particular, it's most important to test whether "alignment techniques" are effective in the broader context of the full training pipeline and deployment ecosystem, especially if they have elements which would likely induce misalignment. This is in contrast to simply testing alignment techniques in isolation.
  • Contend with pessimistic assumptions. It is important to highlight the ways alignment strategies will break under pressure—there will be a lot of pressure!
    It's easy to study alignment strategies under optimistic / easy conditions and come away with positive results. However, the same alignment strategies could fall apart under more stringent / suboptimal conditions. As we develop AGI, it is not sufficient to only show cleaned up, best-case examples of techniques working (like this, this, or this).[5]
  • Be as transparent as possible. Consider two possible worlds:
    • Alignment is falling behind capabilities. In this case, society deserves to know as soon as possible. Improving the state of public evidence can build consensus towards a coordinated global slowdown / pause, and buy ourselves time to improve alignment for real.
    • There’s a way to make alignment keep pace with capabilities. In this case, society also deserves to know! If we discover a silver bullet for alignment, then the underlying science should be shared broadly, so that organizations developing powerful AI outside the frontier labs do not build heavily misaligned models.

Total research transparency is also a key component in Plan A from AI 2040.

Specific directions we're excited about

Given the above context, the Arcadia Impact alignment team is currently working on the following technical topics. We would appreciate feedback on whether people think other things should be a higher priority:

Studying how RL affects motivations. It seems like scaling up reinforcement learning leads to many of the failure modes we see in present-day models: reward hacking, motivated reasoning, metagaming, and perhaps instrumental convergence. We require a better understanding of whether these are resolvable issues, as well as a better understanding of how to differentiate principled solutions from patchwork ones.

Stress-testing scalable monitoring. The volume of work done by agents will grow by many orders of magnitude in the future. We'll increasingly rely on scalable monitoring protocols to tell us what's going on. It would be very bad if we were overconfident in how well these protocols work. This will become especially important once we start deploying models on tasks that lack an easily-verifiable ground truth.

Anticipating how prosaic RSI goes wrong. Eventually, models will be put into automated research harnesses even if they're misaligned, either by accident (misalignment was not detected) or intentionally (labs decide to compromise on safety). What are the ways this could play out? This is the least conceptually clear of our directions, due to high uncertainty about what research automation actually looks like. Still, we think it's valuable to do carefully designed experiments comparing aligned and misaligned models in order to surface some broad phenomena.

Thanks to Brandon Riggs, Joe Hardie, Sid Baines, Angel Martinez, Moritz Pfau, Francis Rhys Ward, Emma Mouliere, Jonathan Bostock and Alex Beat for comments/discussion.

    2. All of the doubts about the future are speculation, so there is no legitimate reason to pause current RSI efforts.
    3. Labs have incentives to notice if their internal alignment is truly insufficient.
    4. Even though the current pace of AI development is untenable, we would need cooperation with X entity to enact meaningful safeguards and we are unlikely to get that cooperation.
    5. AI will not reach superintelligent levels or be intelligent enough to be beyond human oversight / affect the real world.
